Linear Regression
Predicting one number from another, step by step
Definition
What is linear regression?
Linear regression predicts a number (the output y) from other numbers (the inputs x) by fitting a straight line to data.
The input
x: what we know
In our story: hours studied.
The output
y: what we predict
In our story: marks scored.
The line
ŷ = b₀ + b₁x
b₀ and b₁ are learned from the data.

14 / 33
Derivation, step 1
The intercept
∂SSE/∂b₀ = −2 Σ (yᵢ − b₀ − b₁xᵢ) = 0
Σ eᵢ = 0 (the residuals add to zero)
Σyᵢ − n·b₀ − b₁Σxᵢ = 0
ȳ = b₀ + b₁x̄
b₀ = ȳ − b₁x̄
So the least squares line always passes through the point of averages (x̄, ȳ).
Linear regression
15 / 33
Derivation, step 2
The slope
∂SSE/∂b₁ = −2 Σ xᵢ (yᵢ − b₀ − b₁xᵢ) = 0
Put in b₀ = ȳ − b₁x̄:
Σ (xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ) = b₁ Σ (xᵢ − x̄)²
b₁ = Σ (xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ) / Σ (xᵢ − x̄)²

Intercept
b₀ = ȳ − b₁x̄
The line passes through (x̄, ȳ).
Equivalent form: b₁ = r · (s_y / s_x), the correlation times the ratio of spreads.

25 / 33
The formula
R²: regression versus naive
Naive: SST = Σ (yᵢ − ȳ)² = 1228
Regression: SSE = Σ eᵢ² = 178
Error removed = SST − SSE = 1050
R² = 1 − SSE / SST
= 1 − 178 / 1228 = 0.855
Conclusion: the regression guesser removes about 85% of the naive guesser’s error.

9 / 32
From S to a line
How does the log of odds turn the S into a line?
Each point on the S moves to a new height: p becomes ln( p / (1 − p) ).
p = 0.1 → −2.2, p = 0.5 → 0, p = 0.9 → +2.2
The S unrolls into a straight line.

The error
How do we estimate b₀ and b₁?
Now we use each data point to estimate b₀ and b₁.
In linear regression we did this with the SSE: the difference between the actual y and ŷ, squared and added up over all the points.
SSE = Σ (y − ŷ)²
How do we find the error here?
Logistic regression
13 / 32
The error
What are the actual and the predicted values?
error = actual (from the data) − predicted
Actual: y = 1 (passed) or 0 (failed)
Predicted: the log of odds, ln( p / (1 − p) ) = z = b₀ + b₁x
So we find p from the log of odds using this equation:
p = 1 / (1 + e−z)
found by solving ln( p / (1 − p) ) = z for p
For the given data, we start by assuming values of b₀ and b₁, and then find the error.

19 / 32
The error
How do we combine all ten students?
The chance given to all ten results is the product of the ten chances: q₁ × q₂ × … × q₁₀
But we want errors to add up, like squared errors do.
The logarithm turns a product into a sum: ln(q₁ × q₂) = ln q₁ + ln q₂
Check: q₁ = 0.9 and q₂ = 0.8. Product 0.72, −ln 0.72 = 0.329 = 0.105 + 0.223
error = −ln(q)
The minus sign makes the error positive, and 0 when q = 1.

b₀ up by 1: every student’s z goes up by 1.
b₁ up by 1: each student’s z goes up by their hours x.
Positive miss: the student wants z up. Negative miss: z down.
b₀ moves every z equally, so each vote counts once: push on b₀ = Σ (y − p) = A
b₁ moves z by x, so a vote counts x times: push on b₁ = Σ (y − p)·x = B
Logistic regression
23 / 32
Fitting
Why is the miss exactly the right vote?
One student: E = −[ y ln p + (1 − y) ln(1 − p) ], p = 1 / (1 + e−z), z = b₀ + b₁x
dE/dp = −y/p + (1 − y)/(1 − p)
dp/dz = p (1 − p)
dE/dz = [ −y/p + (1 − y)/(1 − p) ] · p (1 − p) = p − y
dz/db₀ = 1, dz/db₁ = x ⇒ dE/db₀ = p − y, dE/db₁ = (p − y)·x
Adding over the students, the slope of the total error is −A for b₀ and −B for b₁. Downhill: b₀ ← b₀ + 0.02·A, b₁ ← b₁ + 0.02·B
Check: raising b₀ by 0.01 lowers the total error by 0.0042 (A × 0.01 = 0.0042). Raising b₁ by 0.001 lowers it by 0.0038 (B × 0.001 = 0.0038).
Logistic regression
24 / 32
Fitting
Which way should b₀ and b₁ move?
Push on b₀: A = Σ (y − p) = 0.424
5 students passed, but the model expected only 4.58 passes. Too low overall, so raise b₀.
Push on b₁: B = Σ (y − p)·x = 3.803
The passers studied 37 hours in total, but the model expected 33.2. Make the curve steeper, so raise b₁.
Take a small step: b₀ ← b₀ + 0.02 × A = −2.992 b₁ ← b₁ + 0.02 × B = 0.576
New total error: 4.394, lower than 4.503.
These pushes are the slope of the total error, which works out to exactly the miss y − p.

31 / 32
Summary
What to remember
01
The model: the log-odds are a straight line, z = b₀ + b₁x, turned into a chance by the sigmoid.
02
The error: −ln of the chance the model gave to what really happened.
03
The fit: find p, add up the misses (y − p), nudge b₀ and b₁, and repeat until both pushes are 0.
04
Using it: read the chance, apply a threshold for a yes or no, and compare with the naive guesser.
